summary: We developed a simple video game for young kids ages 7-12 to experience life on the moon and the challenges that come with it. Our goal was to make a game where kids were able to see that even in a game, it’s impossible to have everything and exist in an ideal world, which many children wonder about. This addresses the challenge because it’s a platform that connects real space information and data with entertainment. Our hope is that this game is both engaging and educational for children. As a society, we often underestimate children’s abilities to learn and hinder their ability to grow. This game throws that away–despite the simple interface, they are given real NASA and space facts throughout the game and tested on it to ensure they understand the “why” behind all of these missions. We challenge kids with real decision making and real consequences to those decisions. This engaging project bridges the gap between newer generations and the decades of scientific research, paving the path for future scientists, engineers, and astronauts.
details:
Junior Astronaut

Our project has two main components: software in the form of the game and hardware in the form of a controller. 

The software is a web based game coded in VSCode using TypeScript, React and NextJS, later deployed on Vercel. In the game, users play as an astronaut going on a space mission to the moon. The game goes through four stages before the ultimate challenge.

Stage 1: Go

Players prepare for takeoff by collecting necessary materials including air, battery, and fuel.

Stage 2: Land

Here, players learn how to set up a base and the importance of allocating limited resources. 

Stage 3: Live

At this stage, players set up a farm and learn to plant food through a slow and tedious process, as farming typically is. 

Stage 4: Explore

Finally, players collect necessary rocks for research with limited energy in their rovers. 

Through these stages, players learn the importance of choosing what is most important. Though they may want to bring both a camera to document scientific findings, they could instead bring a battery that would greatly help their survival up on the moon. Similarly, they have to make a choice between barely making it back to base alive or giving up on valuable research material. We factored in real choices that astronauts may have to face in space to make it as realistic as possible. These difficult questions force players to weigh their choices and make the most optimal choice. We wanted the kids to leave this game realizing that they are expected to make smart decisions rather than just believe the game was simply making them do that for no good reason. 

This is why at the end of each stage, they are quizzed with a question regarding certain challenges they faced during the stage, prompting reflection and provoking thoughts about why space missions are the way they are. These are accompanied by fact cards that pop up throughout the game informing players the reason behind each activity they are performing. 

After these preparatory phases, they face the final challenge: keeping themselves and a crew alive for 6 days on the moon while managing their base, planting food, collecting data, and defending against solar storms. This game aims to impact players by forcing them to reconcile with the fact that they can’t have everything. Once players learn this crucial piece of information, they can learn to make optimal choices and develop better decision making skills. One big factor that we considered was retention. We wanted to make sure there was a fair balance between easy and difficult to make players inclined to stay. This game isn’t hard to get the hang of, but it also isn’t excruciatingly simple, so it forces players to stay engaged and progress to higher levels, collecting stars and trophies along the way. 

The hardware of this project was created using an ESP-32. It was coded with C++ through Wokwi and simulations were also run in there to preserve time rather than rewiring the actual board. The code was then compiled in Wokwi and put into esptool in order to program it onto the ESP-32. The connected components consisted of a joystick, four buttons, an LCD, and two LEDs. 

The joystick acted as the primary method for clicking things as well as a cursor in order to make navigating easier when there are so many things to click. The four buttons controlled “WASD” on the keyboard, making it easy to control the movements. The LCD notifies the player when the controller is connected to the game and displays the name of each level so the player stays aware. The LEDs were planned to light up red when there are dangers present in the final level and when you lose hearts and light up green when everything is safe. 

The case of the controller and the button extenders were made on Fusion360 and sliced through the MultiMaker Digital Factory because we used a MakerBot Replicator+ printer with PLA. Though the sizing of this case was made largely with the size of the breadboard, ESP-32, and LCD in mind, it was also created with children in mind. We opted to make it smaller because children’s hands are smaller with rounded sides to ensure a comfortable grip. The reason we created a case at all was because we understood that children could not play a game through a bunch of wires and they had to be encased in order to have a seamless gaming experience. Having a controller always enhances a gaming experience, making it feel much more legitimate than a regular browser game, and we hoped that this would encourage kids to play this game more often and as a result, learn more. 

All in all, this project combines software and hardware to create a gaming experience for children 7-12 (though players of all ages can find enjoyment here) to learn more about NASA, space exploration, and the importance of careful decision making. Every decision is creative, and this game stimulates their brains through the gameplay. Unlike any other educational game, we made the information feel natural, rather than a forced addition. Through pop-ups and motivational quizzes, we encourage learning in children of all ages. We hope this game impacts these children positively and teaches them an important lesson they will carry onto their future, whether that’s in the aerospace industry or not.
